title: Mapping open quantum dynamics onto graphs
authors: Kyuho Kim, Dayeong Lee, Seungkyun Park, Xianji Piao, Namkyoo Park, Sunkyu Yu
abstract: Graph-theoretic frameworks have been widely employed in quantum physics to address the high-dimensional complexity of quantum systems. Although open quantum dynamics incorporates system-bath coupling via numerous interacting operators, it has been formulated algebraically with a partial set of jump operators or statistically universal reservoirs, leaving the underlying connectivity structure largely unexplored. Here, we propose a universal graph-theoretic framework for Markovian quantum dynamics. The framework maps open quantum dynamics onto two uniquely defined graphs, where the quantum master equation is rigorously interpreted as the average wave characteristic of operator-valued signals across the graphs. Applying this framework to the open quantum Rabi model, we demonstrate an open-system generalization of Fock-state lattices, characterize graph-topological signatures of dissipation, and classify the weak-to-ultrastrong coupling transition. Building on these representations, graph pruning reveals the backbone of open quantum dynamics, which enables superior graph neural-network learning. Our results bridge graph theory and open quantum dynamics, achieving efficient data-driven analysis of high-dimensional complexity.
summary: The paper introduces a universal graph-theoretic framework to model open quantum dynamics by mapping the system's evolution onto two interconnected graphs. By applying this to the Open Quantum Rabi Model, the authors characterize how dissipation manifests as unique topological signatures within these graphs. This approach allows for efficient data-driven analysis and prediction of complex spectral properties using Graph Neural Networks.
main_problem: To develop a universal graph-theoretic framework for mapping and analyzing both isolated and open quantum dynamics, specifically addressing the unexplored connectivity structure arising from system-bath coupling.
main_result: The authors successfully map open quantum dynamics onto two distinct graphs ($G_H$ and $G_L$), providing a rigorous mathematical tool to characterize dissipation signatures and enabling data-driven analysis via graph neural networks.
method: The framework constructs Schrödinger operator graphs for the unitary part and uses a second graph derived from the Kossakowski matrix for the nonunitary (dissipative) evolution, allowing spectral analysis and machine learning prediction of Liouville spectra.
model_or_system: The study focuses on open quantum systems governed by Markovian dynamics, exemplified by the Open Quantum Rabi Model (QRM), which includes coupling strengths ($\kappa, \gamma, \gamma_\phi$) and dissipation parameters.
key_observables: Liouville spectra ($\lambda$), graph-topological signatures of dissipation, Fiedler value ($\lambda_1$), and spectral distance measures like the Chamfer distance ($D$).
important_parameters: Coupling strengths ($\kappa, \gamma, \gamma_\phi$), pruning thresholds ($\chi$), and system size parameters ($N_{max}$). The analysis covers weak-to-ultrastrong coupling (USC) transitions.
main_assumptions: The framework relies on using the first standard form of the Lindblad QME to ensure all degrees of freedom are encoded in the graph structures, and it compares graph pruning against matrix sparsification techniques.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the constructed Schrödinger operator graphs ($G_H$ and $G_L$) for the open QRM under various coupling regimes. They show spectral comparisons using Liouville spectra ($\lambda$), demonstrating that graph pruning preserves spectral features better than direct matrix pruning, and present GCN training results.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the universal graph framework by defining two graphs ($G_H$ and $G_L$) representing unitary and nonunitary evolution. It applies this to the QRM, analyzing dissipation signatures and USC transitions using graph metrics. Finally, it develops and validates a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) trained on these graph representations to predict the Liouville spectrum.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, unifying mathematical language—graph theory—to analyze complex open quantum dynamics, bridging abstract topological concepts with concrete physical phenomena like dissipation and coupling regime transitions in cavity QED systems.
